program: Inglês Geral & Intercultural -- Fluência e Autonomia
hub_subtitle: Inglês para a vida real — falar, entender qualquer sotaque e ter autonomia no idioma

lesson.menu_desc: Everything from lessons 1 to 7 in one place, and the first real benchmark: three minutes of your own English, timed
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 8 -- Checkpoint -- Block 1
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Claudia Veraldi | Lesson 8 -- Checkpoint -- Block 1

listenings.text: I have been speaking English at work for nineteen years and I have never once been mistaken for a native speaker. For a long time I thought that was the problem. Then a colleague from Lisbon said something to me that I still think about. She said, nobody in this room is grading your grammar. They are waiting to hear what you think. And she was right. In nineteen years, not one person has ever said to me, your English is not good enough. What they have said is, sorry, I did not follow that part. Which is a completely different problem, and a much easier one to fix. So my advice, off the top of my head, is this. Be concise. Stop when the point is made. And when you lose the word, do not stop talking. Go around it.

My teacher asked me to talk for three minutes about my own life, without notes, and I want to tell you what happened, because it was not what I expected. The first minute was terrible. I was translating in my head and I was long-winded and I said the same thing three times. Somewhere in the second minute something changed. I stopped listening to myself. I was just talking, and I was making mistakes, and it did not matter, because she was following me. Come to think of it, that was the first conversation in English where I forgot that it was English. The third minute went by and I did not notice. When she stopped me, I had said more than I say in most meetings. Looking back on it, that exercise was the milestone. Not a test I passed. A thing I stopped being afraid of.

defs: Saying a lot in very few words
To move away from the subject you were talking about

vocab.text: Every word here is about MANAGING your own turn, not about being correct. That is the whole difference between lesson one and lesson eight: you already have the grammar. Tonight you learn what to do while you are using it.

reading.rtitle: What Seven Lessons Actually Bought You
paras: It is tempting to measure a language course in structures. Seven lessons, seven grammar points, tick them off. That is not what changed, and it is worth being precise about what did, because the next thirty-two lessons depend on knowing it.

What changed is the size of the thing you can hold. In lesson one you answered a question. By lesson six you told a two-year story with a background and a turning point, and the listener knew exactly which morning it turned. That is not a grammar point. That is a longer turn, and a longer turn is the only real measure of level.

The second thing that changed is quieter. You have listened to an Indian colleague, a Norwegian, a Dutchman, an Italian, a German, a Briton and an Australian, and you understood all of them. Most learners spend years believing that the goal is to understand a film. The goal is to understand the person in the room, and the person in the room is almost never from a film.

What has not changed, and will not, is that you will keep losing words in the middle of sentences. Everybody does, in every language, including the one you were born into. The difference between a B2 speaker and a C1 speaker is not the number of words lost. It is what happens in the second after the word disappears: the B2 stops, and the C1 goes around it and keeps the turn.

reading.prompt: Read once, quickly. Which title fits the whole text best?
choices: Seven grammar points and how to remember them
What grew is the length of the turn you can hold, and what matters is what you do when a word disappears
Why understanding films is the real goal

items: The text says the real measure of level is the number of grammar points you know.
It says a longer turn is the only real measure of level, and that a grammar point is not what changed.
By lesson six she could tell a story with a background and a turning point.
And the listener knew exactly which morning it turned — which is a longer turn, not a structure.
The text says the goal is to understand a film.
The opposite: the goal is to understand the person in the room, who is almost never from a film.
Losing words in the middle of a sentence will stop happening at C1.
It says everybody loses words, in every language, including their first one.
What separates B2 from C1 is what you do in the second after a word disappears.
The B2 stops; the C1 goes around it and keeps the turn.

items.situation: Somebody asks who you are, and you are not allowed to say your job title. Fifteen seconds.
tips: I have lived in the countryside since 2021, and before that I spent forty years in a city of twenty million.
Lesson 1: present perfect for what continues, plain past for what finished.

items.situation: Compare where you live now with where you lived before, and do not use the word better.
tips: It is far quieter, and nowhere near as convenient.
Lesson 2: far, nowhere near as, by far — the boosters, not the plain comparative.

items.situation: Somebody asks how long you have been working on the house, and what is finished.
tips: I have been restoring it since 2021, and I have finished the kitchen and both bedrooms.
Lesson 3: how long takes the -ing one, how much is done takes the other.

items.situation: You miss a whole sentence in a meeting with somebody you have met once. Ask again.
tips: Sorry, I did not catch that. Could you say it again?
Lesson 4: the neutral one works everywhere. Never What? on its own.

items.situation: Describe one person from your town, with two adjectives, in the order English expects.
tips: There is a gruff old Italian cheese seller with a weathered face.
Lesson 5: opinion, then age, then origin — and the noun keeps its closest friend.

items.situation: Tell the morning you decided to leave, with the background and the event in one sentence.
tips: I was sitting in gridlock one Tuesday when I finally snapped.
Lesson 6: was or were plus -ing for the background, plain past for the event that cut it.

items.situation: Say what has been done to the house and what is being done right now, without naming anybody.
tips: The plaster was removed by hand and the kitchen is being rewired at the moment.
Lesson 7: be plus the participle, and the name only comes back when it matters.

answerkey.title: Reveal the whole block-one key
key: Lesson 1 — what continues vs what finished: I have lived here since 2021 · I lived there for forty years
Lesson 2 — the boosters: far quieter · nowhere near as busy · by far the best decision
Lesson 3 — how long vs how much: I have been restoring it since 2021 · I have finished the kitchen
Lesson 4 — the neutral repair: Sorry, I did not catch that. Could you say it again?
Lesson 5 — the order, and the pair: a gruff old Italian seller · it is tiring, I am tired
Lesson 6 — background and event: I was sitting in gridlock when I snapped
Lesson 7 — the passive: it was built in 1932 · it is being rewired · it has been treated twice
And the one that is not grammar: when the word disappears, go around it and keep the turn.
